title: The multiplication rule
objectives: Find $P(A \cap B)$ as $P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$ for draws in sequence
Chain the rule across three draws, and see that either order gives the same answer
Recognise when the plain product $P(A)\,P(B)$ is wrong

screens.title: The multiplication rule
screens.prose: Deal two cards and the second deal meets a smaller deck. We will chain the chances of draws made one after another.
A small deck holds four hearts and two spades. Cards are written 9H for the 9 of hearts. Two cards are dealt, one after the other, and none goes back. The first card is 9H.
screens.question: Tap every card that would make the second card a heart.

hints.text: Which cards are still in the deck?
9H has gone, so one heart fewer is left.
Three hearts are left: 2H, 5H and JH. Tap those.

feedback.correct: Three hearts are left among 5 cards.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the hearts still in the deck, and only those.

byKey.all-left: You tapped every card left. A spade would make the second card a spade.
byKey.s3: 3S is a spade, so it would make the second card a spade.
byKey.s8: 8S is a spade, so it would make the second card a spade.

explain.text: You tapped 3 hearts among the 5 cards left. So the second card is a heart with chance $\tfrac{3}{5}$, not $\tfrac{4}{6}$. The first deal took one heart and one card out of the count.

screens.prose: Same deck, a fresh deal. This time the first card is 3S. Tap a card to mark it, and tap it again to clear it.
screens.question: Tap every card that would make the second card a heart.

hints.text: Which cards did the first deal leave?
Only one spade is left in the deck.

feedback.correct: All four hearts are left, among 5 cards.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap every heart still in the deck.

byKey.with-spade: You tapped 8S as well. It would make the second card a spade.
byKey.s8: 8S is a spade, so it would make the second card a spade.

explain.text: A spade first leaves every heart in the deck, so the chance is $\tfrac{4}{5}$. A heart first left only $\tfrac{3}{5}$. The second deal's chance depends on what the first deal took.

screens.prose: Now ask before any card is dealt. The first card is a heart with chance $\tfrac{4}{6}$. Chaining that with the next chance, counted on what is left, is the **multiplication rule**: $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$$

state.caption: Two deals from 6 cards, none put back

screens.question: What is the chance both cards are hearts? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: A heart comes first $\tfrac{4}{6}$ of the time. In what share of those is the second a heart too?
The second factor is counted on the 5 cards the first heart leaves.
Multiply: $\tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{3}{5} = \tfrac{12}{30}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the first heart's chance by the second's, counted on what is left.

byKey.fixed: That is $\tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{4}{6}$. You kept 6 cards and 4 hearts for the second deal.
byKey.second-only: That is the second deal given a heart first. Multiply by the chance the first is a heart.
byKey.first-only: That is only the first card. The second must be a heart too, so the chance shrinks.
byKey.after-spade: You used $\tfrac{4}{5}$, the chance after a spade. Here the first card is a heart.

explain.text: A heart comes first in $\tfrac{4}{6}$ of deals, and $\tfrac{3}{5}$ of those continue with a heart. So $P(\text{both hearts}) = \tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{3}{5} = \tfrac{2}{5}$. The second factor is a conditional probability, counted on the smaller deck.

canvas.caption: After one heart: 3 hearts among 5 cards

screens.prose: Deal a third card from the same deck. The picture shows the deck after two hearts.

state.caption: After two hearts: 2 hearts among 4 cards

screens.question: Before any deal, what is the chance all three cards are hearts? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance all three cards are hearts

hints.text: Chain one more factor onto $\tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{3}{5}$.
The third factor is counted on the 4 cards left after two hearts.
$\tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{3}{5} \times \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{24}{120}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Chain three factors, each counted on what the earlier deals left.

byKey.fixed: That is $\tfrac{4}{6}$ three times. Each deal meets a smaller deck with fewer hearts.
byKey.two-only: That stops after two cards. The third must be a heart too, so multiply by $\tfrac{2}{4}$.
byKey.last-only: That is the third deal given two hearts. Multiply by the chance of the first two hearts.

explain.text: Each new factor is counted on what the earlier deals left: $\tfrac{4}{6}$, then $\tfrac{3}{5}$, then $\tfrac{2}{4}$. The product is $\tfrac{24}{120} = \tfrac{1}{5}$. Three events chain the same way two do.

screens.prose: Change the game. After each deal the card goes back, and the deck is shuffled before the next deal.

enter.caption: 9H goes back: 6 cards and 4 hearts again

screens.question: What is the chance both cards are hearts now? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance both cards are hearts, with replacement

hints.text: After the first heart goes back, what does the deck look like?
The deck is whole again for the second deal.
The second factor is $\tfrac{4}{6}$ again: $\tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{4}{6} = \tfrac{16}{36}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The card goes back, so count the second deal on the whole deck.

byKey.took-out: You took the first heart out of the deck. It went back, so the second deal sees 4 hearts among 6.
byKey.first-only: That is one card. Both must be hearts, so multiply by a second factor.
byKey.added: You added the two chances, and a chance above 1 is impossible. A sequence multiplies.

explain.text: With the card back, $P(\text{2nd heart} \mid \text{1st heart}) = \tfrac{4}{6}$, the same as with no news. So the rule becomes a plain product: $\tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{4}{6} = \tfrac{4}{9}$. This is the edge case where $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$.

screens.prose: Back to dealing without replacement. Sam says the first card is a heart with chance $\tfrac{4}{6}$, and so is the second, seen alone. So both are hearts with chance $\tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{4}{6}$.

state.caption: 30 possible deals: a card cannot come out twice

screens.question: What is the chance both cards are hearts?

options.why: You multiplied two chances that are each right alone. After a heart, the second is a heart with chance $\tfrac{3}{5}$, not $\tfrac{4}{6}$.

canvas.caption: $\tfrac{16}{36}$ counts the diagonal, where one card is dealt twice

options.why: You used $\tfrac{4}{5}$ for the second card. That is its chance after a spade, but here the first card is a heart.
That is the chance of one heart. Both cards must be hearts.

hints.text: Count the deals where both cards are hearts, out of the 30 possible.
Both-heart deals sit in the top-left block, off the blank diagonal.
Rows 2H to JH meet columns 2H to JH in 16 cells. Take away the 4 blank ones: 12 of 30.

feedback.correct: 12 of the 30 deals are both hearts: $\tfrac{2}{5}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the both-heart deals off the blank diagonal, out of 30.

byKey.sam: You multiplied $\tfrac{4}{6}$ by $\tfrac{4}{6}$, as Sam did. Seen alone, the second card is a heart $\tfrac{4}{6}$ of the time, but not after a heart.

explain.text: Sam's $\tfrac{4}{6}$ for the second card is right only when the first is unseen. Once the first is a heart, 3 hearts sit among 5 cards, so the factor is $\tfrac{3}{5}$. His $\tfrac{16}{36}$ counts the blank diagonal, where one card is dealt twice.

screens.prose: Every chain you built took one factor per deal, each counted on the deck as it stood. $$P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)\,P(C \mid A \cap B)$$ With replacement, each factor is the plain chance.
screens.question: Which product gives a heart, then a spade, then a heart?

options.why: You kept the deck whole for every deal. Each deal leaves one card fewer.
You took two hearts out. The second card was a spade, so 3 hearts are left.
You took a heart out but kept 5 cards for the third deal. Two cards are gone, so 4 are left.

hints.text: What is left in the deck after a heart, then a spade?
After a heart and a spade, 4 cards are left: 3 hearts and 1 spade.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each deal on what the earlier deals left.

explain.text: After a heart, 2 spades sit among 5 cards: $\tfrac{2}{5}$. After the spade too, 3 hearts sit among 4 cards: $\tfrac{3}{4}$. The chain gives $\tfrac{24}{120} = \tfrac{1}{5}$.

screens.prose: Let $A$ be a heart first and $B$ a spade second. By rows, $P(A)\,P(B \mid A) = \tfrac{4}{6} \times \tfrac{2}{5} = \tfrac{8}{30}$. Now count by columns: $$\frac{8}{30} = P(B)\,P(A \mid B) = \frac{10}{30} \times \;?$$

state.caption: Outlined: a spade second. Shaded: a heart first as well

screens.question: What is $P(A \mid B)$, the missing factor?

hints.text: How many outlined cells are there, and how many of them are shaded?
The outline holds every deal with a spade second.
10 cells have a spade second, and 8 of them have a heart first: $\tfrac{8}{10}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded cells inside the outlined columns.

byKey.unconditional: $\tfrac{4}{6}$ is the chance of a heart first with no news. Inside the spade columns, 8 of 10 deals start with a heart.
byKey.upside-down: That factor is upside down. It would make the product bigger than $\tfrac{10}{30}$.
byKey.rows: $\tfrac{2}{5}$ is $P(B \mid A)$ from the rows. You need the chance of $A$ inside the columns.

explain.text: Inside the 10 deals with a spade second, 8 have a heart first, so $P(A \mid B) = \tfrac{4}{5}$. Both orders give $\tfrac{8}{30}$, because $P(A \mid B) = \tfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$ multiplies out with either event as the condition. So $P(A)\,P(B \mid A) = P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)$.

screens.prose: Your orders fill against five counterparties. Last month counterparty A supplied 40% of your fills. Flow comes in clusters: after a fill from A, the next fill is from A 60% of the time.

state.caption: Share of last month’s fills by counterparty

screens.question: What is the chance the next two fills both come from A? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance the next two fills both come from A

hints.text: Which chance is for the first fill, and which for the second?
The first fill is from A with chance 0.4.
Given the first is from A, the second is from A with chance 0.6. Multiply: $0.4 \times 0.6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Chain the first fill's chance with the second's, given the first.

byKey.unrelated: You used 0.4 twice, as if fills were unrelated. After a fill from A, the next is from A with chance 0.6.
byKey.second-only: That is the second fill given the first. Multiply by 0.4, the chance the first is from A.
byKey.added: You added 0.4 and 0.6. Along a sequence, chances multiply.

explain.text: The first fill is from A with chance 0.4, and the second follows with chance 0.6: $0.4 \times 0.6 = 0.24$. Treating the fills as unrelated gives $0.4 \times 0.4 = 0.16$. That understates the clustering by a third.

ideas: Each draw is counted on what the earlier draws left.
The chance of a sequence is a chain of factors, $P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$, and either order gives $P(A \cap B)$.
With replacement every factor is the plain chance, so the rule becomes a plain product.

formula.name: Multiplication rule
formula.tex: P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)
formula.note: For three events, chain one more factor: $P(C \mid A \cap B)$.

summary.trap: $P(A)\,P(B)$ is wrong when the first draw changes the second. Count the second factor on what is left.

quiz.prose: A loan book holds 12 loans, and 3 are in arrears. An auditor picks two different loans at random, one after the other.
quiz.question: What is the chance both picks are in arrears? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance both loans are in arrears

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the second pick on the 11 loans left.

byKey.fixed: That is $\tfrac{3}{12} \times \tfrac{3}{12}$. The first loan is not picked again, so 2 of 11 are left.
byKey.second-only: That is the second pick given the first. Multiply by $\tfrac{3}{12}$.

explain.text: The first pick is in arrears with chance $\tfrac{3}{12}$. That leaves 2 such loans among 11. So both are with chance $\tfrac{3}{12} \times \tfrac{2}{11} = \tfrac{1}{22}$.

quiz.prose: Two cards are dealt from a standard 52-card deck, without replacement.
quiz.question: What is the chance the first is an ace and the second is a king?

options.why: You used 52 cards for both deals. After the ace, 51 are left.
You took the first card out of the kings, but it was an ace. All 4 kings are still there.
You added the two chances. Both deals must happen, so the chances multiply.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the king on the 51 cards the ace leaves.

explain.text: The first card is an ace with chance $\tfrac{4}{52}$. The ace leaves 51 cards, all 4 kings among them. So the chance is $\tfrac{4}{52} \times \tfrac{4}{51} = \tfrac{16}{2652} = \tfrac{4}{663}$.

quiz.prose: A card is drawn from a standard deck, put back, and the deck is shuffled. Then a second card is drawn.
quiz.question: What is the chance both cards are hearts?

options.why: You kept the first heart out. It went back, so the second draw sees 13 hearts among 52.
You added $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$. Both draws must be hearts, so multiply.
That is the chance for one card. Both must be hearts.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The card goes back, so the second draw meets the whole deck.

explain.text: Putting the card back restores the deck, so $P(\text{2nd heart} \mid \text{1st heart}) = \tfrac{1}{4}$. The rule becomes a plain product: $\tfrac{1}{4} \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{16}$.

quiz.prose: A desk has 5 traders: 3 senior and 2 junior. Three are picked in turn, at random, for the weekend rota.
quiz.question: What is the chance all three picks are senior? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance all three picks are senior

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Chain three factors, each counted on the traders left.

byKey.fixed: That is $(\tfrac{3}{5})^3$. A trader picked once cannot be picked again.
byKey.two-only: That stops after two picks. Multiply by $\tfrac{1}{3}$ for the third.

explain.text: The first pick is senior with chance $\tfrac{3}{5}$, the second $\tfrac{2}{4}$, the third $\tfrac{1}{3}$. The chain gives $\tfrac{6}{60} = \tfrac{1}{10}$.
